rule_sets.title: NSW: houses, extensions and granny flats
rule_sets.description: Approval pathways in New South Wales for new houses, extensions and secondary dwellings: exempt development, complying development certificates, development applications and the certificates that follow.
limitations: We don't know your zone or your council's Local Environmental Plan (LEP), so we can't say which pathway applies, only which ones may.
We don't check the development standards in the complying development codes (setbacks, height, site coverage, landscaping).
Constraints like heritage, bush fire and flooding come from your answers. Your section 10.7 planning certificate is the official record.
Not legal advice. Confirm with your council, a registered certifier or a town planner before you rely on it.

rules.title: A complying development certificate may be possible
rules.notes: Every house, extension or granny flat in NSW starts here. Certainty is MAY_APPLY because we don't know the zone or whether every code standard is met.

outcomes.title: You may be able to use the fast-track complying development pathway (CDC)
outcomes.detail: A complying development certificate (CDC) is planning and building approval in one. Your council or a registered certifier can issue it, usually in about 20 days (10 days for NSW Housing Pattern Book designs), if the work meets every standard in a State code: the Housing Code for houses and extensions, the Low Rise Housing Diversity Code for dual occupancies and terraces, or the Housing SEPP for granny flats. It is not available on heritage items, in environmentally sensitive areas or at BAL-40 or flame zone bush fire risk. If any standard is not met, you need a development application instead.

approval.authority: Your council or a registered certifier
approval.pathway: Complying development under the Codes SEPP or Housing SEPP 2021

evidence.title: Site plan with setbacks, heights and existing buildings
Section 10.7 planning certificate for the lot

payload.task: Ask a registered certifier whether your design meets the complying development code

rules.title: A development application is needed if a CDC doesn't fit

outcomes.title: If your project isn't exempt or complying development, you need a development application (DA)
outcomes.detail: Most building work that can't meet a complying development code needs development consent from your council. You lodge the DA on the NSW Planning Portal with plans, a statement of environmental effects, owner's consent and a cost estimate. Whether your zone allows the use comes from the council's Local Environmental Plan (LEP), which we haven't checked.

approval.pathway: Development application (local development) on the NSW Planning Portal

evidence.title: Signed consent of every owner of the land

payload.task: Check your zone and controls on the NSW Planning Portal Spatial Viewer

rules.title: Small works may be exempt development

outcomes.title: Small additions like decks, carports and sheds may need no approval
outcomes.detail: Exempt development needs no planning or building approval if it meets every standard in the Codes SEPP and the Building Code of Australia. Decks, garden sheds, carports, fences and similar small works can qualify. It is not available on State heritage listed land, in critical habitat or wilderness. A habitable room extension is usually not exempt. Check the standards for your exact work before you start.

payload.task: Check the exempt development standards for your work on the NSW Planning Portal

rules.title: Heritage item or conservation area
rules.notes: Clause 1.17A was read directly, but customers can't tell a heritage item from a conservation area, so capped at likely.

outcomes.title: Heritage: you will probably need a development application, not a CDC
outcomes.detail: Complying development can't be carried out on a heritage item listed in the State Heritage Register or in the council's LEP. In a heritage conservation area the codes also restrict complying development. Your section 10.7 planning certificate says which applies. Expect council to ask for a heritage impact statement.

approval.pathway: Development application (heritage item or conservation area)

payload.task: Order a section 10.7 planning certificate to confirm the heritage listing

outcomes.title: Flooding: a CDC is only possible if the flood control lot rules are met
outcomes.detail: If council applies flood-related controls to your lot (a flood control lot), complying development is only possible when extra flood criteria are met, usually with a report from an engineer. Otherwise you need a development application. Your section 10.7 planning certificate says whether flood controls apply.

approval.pathway: DA if the flood control lot criteria for complying development are not met

evidence.title: Flood report or certificate from a suitably qualified engineer

payload.task: Ask council for flood information for your lot

outcomes.title: Bush fire prone land: you need a bush fire assessment
outcomes.detail: On bush fire prone land your application needs a bush fire assessment showing it meets Planning for Bush Fire Protection 2019. For a CDC you need a BAL certificate from council or an accredited bush fire consultant showing the site is BAL-29 or lower. At BAL-40 or the flame zone (BAL-FZ) a CDC is not allowed and you need a development application. Building costs rise with the BAL rating.

approval.authority: Accredited bush fire consultant or council (NSW RFS for referrals)
approval.pathway: Bush fire assessment report or BAL certificate under PBP 2019

evidence.title: Bush fire assessment report or BAL certificate

payload.task: Check whether your land is bush fire prone with the NSW RFS online tool

outcomes.title: If you go the DA route, you need a construction certificate before building
outcomes.detail: After development consent, a construction certificate confirms your building plans match the consent and the Building Code of Australia. Work can't start until it is issued, a principal certifier is appointed and council is told at least 2 days before work starts. You don't need one with a CDC or for exempt work.

approval.authority: Your council or a registered certifier
approval.pathway: Construction certificate on the NSW Planning Portal after development consent

payload.task: Choose and appoint a principal certifier before work starts

outcomes.title: You need an occupation certificate before anyone lives in the new dwelling
outcomes.detail: An occupation certificate must be obtained to occupy and use a new building. Your principal certifier issues it after the final inspection, once the work matches the approval and the BASIX commitments are met.

approval.pathway: Occupation certificate on the NSW Planning Portal

outcomes.title: An occupation certificate may be needed for the new part of the building
outcomes.detail: An occupation certificate is needed to occupy and use a new building or a new part of a building approved by a DA or CDC. Exempt work doesn't need one.

approval.pathway: Occupation certificate on the NSW Planning Portal

outcomes.title: You need a BASIX certificate for a new dwelling
outcomes.detail: Every new home in NSW, including a granny flat, needs a BASIX certificate showing it meets the water, energy and thermal comfort standards. You make it in the online BASIX tool and attach it to your DA or CDC, and again to the construction certificate.

approval.authority: NSW Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure (online BASIX tool)
approval.pathway: NSW BASIX certificate tool on the Planning Portal

payload.task: Create a BASIX certificate before you lodge

outcomes.title: A BASIX certificate is needed if the work costs more than $50,000
outcomes.detail: Renovations and additions costing more than $50,000, and pools or spas of 40,000 litres or more, need a BASIX certificate.

approval.authority: NSW Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure (online BASIX tool)
approval.pathway: NSW BASIX certificate tool on the Planning Portal

rule_sets.title: NSW: secondary dwellings (granny flats)
rule_sets.description: Secondary dwellings under the State Environmental Planning Policy (Housing) 2021.
limitations: Built from the Department's secondary dwellings page and one council page, not from the full text of the Housing SEPP, which we couldn't read.
Doesn't check setbacks, height, private open space or whether your zone permits secondary dwellings.
Not legal advice. Confirm with your council or a registered certifier.

rules.title: Lot size for a granny flat CDC

outcomes.title: Your lot meets the 450 m2 minimum for a granny flat CDC
outcomes.detail: A secondary dwelling can be complying development on a lot of at least 450 m2 if it meets the other Housing SEPP standards, such as floor area, setbacks and height.

outcomes.title: Under 450 m2: a granny flat CDC is not available
outcomes.detail: On a lot smaller than 450 m2 a secondary dwelling can't be complying development unless it is built entirely inside the existing house. You would need a development application, if your council's LEP allows it.

approval.pathway: Development application for a secondary dwelling

payload.task: Ask council whether a secondary dwelling is allowed on your lot

rules.title: Granny flat goes with a main house

outcomes.title: One principal dwelling and one secondary dwelling are allowed
outcomes.detail: A secondary dwelling sits on the same lot as the main home. The lot can have only one of each, and it can't then be subdivided to separate them.

outcomes.title: There is no main house yet
outcomes.detail: A secondary dwelling is defined as being on the same site as a principal dwelling. If there is no house yet, plan both together, for example a new house and granny flat in one application.

rules.title: Granny flat floor area
rules.notes: 60 m2 confirmed only through a council page citing Housing SEPP clause 52; the SEPP text itself could not be read.

outcomes.title: Within the usual 60 m2 limit
outcomes.detail: The Housing SEPP generally limits a secondary dwelling to 60 m2. Some council LEPs allow more.

outcomes.title: Over 60 m2: check your council's limit
outcomes.detail: The Housing SEPP generally limits a secondary dwelling to 60 m2. Some councils allow a larger one (for example the greater of 60 m2 or a share of the main house), but a bigger granny flat may need a DA or may not be allowed.

payload.task: Check the maximum granny flat size with your council

rule_sets.title: NSW: subdivision
rule_sets.description: Subdividing land in New South Wales: development application, bush fire safety authority and subdivision certificate.
limitations: We don't check the minimum lot size in your council's LEP or whether your subdivision could be exempt or complying development.
We don't calculate developer contributions or water and sewer charges.
Not legal advice. Confirm with your council, a surveyor or a town planner.

rules.title: Development application to subdivide
rules.notes: Some subdivision (for example boundary adjustments or some strata subdivision) can be exempt or complying development; not encoded.

outcomes.title: Subdividing land usually needs a development application
outcomes.detail: Creating new lots usually needs development consent from council. The council's LEP sets the minimum lot size for your zone. Council's DA fee for 2026/27 is up to $458 plus $53 per additional lot ($921 plus $65 per lot if a new public road is created). Developer contributions and water and sewer charges may also apply.

approval.pathway: Development application for subdivision on the NSW Planning Portal

evidence.title: Plan of proposed subdivision showing lot areas and dimensions

payload.task: Check the minimum lot size for your zone in the council's LEP

rules.title: Subdivision certificate to register the new lots

outcomes.title: You need a subdivision certificate before the new lots can be registered
outcomes.detail: After the subdivision works are done, a subdivision certificate confirms the consent conditions are met and lets NSW Land Registry Services register the plan, creating the new titles.

approval.authority: Your council or a registered certifier
approval.pathway: Subdivision certificate on the NSW Planning Portal

evidence.title: Final plan of subdivision from a registered surveyor

outcomes.title: Bush fire prone land: the NSW RFS must approve the subdivision
outcomes.detail: Residential subdivision of bush fire prone land needs a bush fire safety authority from the NSW Rural Fire Service. That makes it integrated development: council refers your DA to the RFS, and you pay extra referral fees. Include a bush fire assessment report showing the subdivision meets Planning for Bush Fire Protection 2019.

approval.pathway: Bush fire safety authority (Rural Fires Act s100B), integrated development

evidence.title: Bush fire assessment report for the subdivision

rule_sets.title: NSW: change of use
rule_sets.description: Changing how a building is used in New South Wales: exempt, complying or a development application.
limitations: We can't read your current and proposed uses against the Codes SEPP tables, so all three pathways are shown as possible.
Changing a building's Building Code class (for example to a home or food premises) may also need building work approval and fire safety upgrades.
Not legal advice. Confirm with your council, a registered certifier or a town planner.

rules.title: Change of use within the same business category

outcomes.title: Some changes of use need no approval
outcomes.detail: Under the Codes SEPP, changing between uses in the same business category is exempt development. For example, a shop can become an office or business premises, or one industrial or warehouse use can become another. Changing from one kind of shop to another is a change of tenant, not a change of use. Minor internal work like painting and new carpet can be done at the same time. It isn't available on State heritage listed land.

payload.task: Check the exempt change of use table on the NSW Planning Portal

rules.title: Change of use as complying development

outcomes.title: If it isn't exempt, a CDC may cover the change of use
outcomes.detail: Where a change of use can't meet the exempt standards, it may be complying development under the Codes SEPP, approved by council or a registered certifier. Land exclusions and local variations apply.

approval.authority: Your council or a registered certifier
approval.pathway: Complying development change of use under the Codes SEPP

rules.title: Change of use by development application

outcomes.title: Otherwise, a change of use needs a development application
outcomes.detail: If the new use is neither exempt nor complying development, you need a DA, and the use must be allowed in your zone under the council's LEP. A DA with no building work costs up to $395 in council fees in 2026/27.

approval.pathway: Development application for change of use

evidence.title: Statement of environmental effects describing the new use, hours, staff and parking

payload.task: Check the new use is permitted in your zone in the council's LEP

rule_sets.title: NSW: every planning project
rule_sets.description: Steps that apply to any planning project in New South Wales.
limitations: We don't look up your council or zone. Not legal advice.

outcomes.title: Start with a section 10.7 planning certificate
outcomes.detail: Your council's section 10.7 planning certificate shows the zone and whether heritage, bush fire, flood or other controls apply to the lot. It costs up to $74 ($185 with the extra section 10.7(5) advice) in 2026/27 and you can order it on the NSW Planning Portal. The Planning Portal Spatial Viewer shows zoning for free.

payload.task: Order a section 10.7 planning certificate from your council

outcomes.title: Your project may need a development application
outcomes.detail: In NSW, work is either exempt (no approval), complying development (a CDC from council or a certifier) or needs a development application to council. Check the exempt and complying development codes first. If neither fits, lodge a DA on the NSW Planning Portal.
